abstracts.abstract: This paper presents a paradigm-shifting framework for robot manipulation control that fundamentally reconceptualizes the relationship between model-based control and learning-based adaptation. Traditional approaches treat these as separate components, leading to suboptimal performance in novel scenarios. We propose Physical Prior-Embedded Meta-Reinforcement Learning (P2EMRL), a unified theoretical framework that encodes physical constraints as inductive biases within the meta-learning architecture. The framework establishes rigorous mathematical connections between Lagrangian mechanics and neural network parameterization, enabling robots to rapidly adapt manipulation strategies across varied object geometries and physical properties. We derive convergence guarantees for the meta-training procedure and prove generalization bounds that quantify how physical prior knowledge transfers across task distributions. Extensive simulation and real-world experiments on a 7-DOF manipulator demonstrate that P2EMRL achieves 94% success rate on novel objects within 5 adaptation trials, compared to 67% for state-of-the-art meta-RL methods. The theoretical analysis reveals that physical priors reduce sample complexity by a factor of 3.7 while maintaining stability margins comparable to traditional MPC. This work establishes a new methodological paradigm that bridges the gap between first-principles control theory and data-driven learning, with implications for autonomous robots operating in unstructured environments.

This paper addresses the fundamental limitation of existing Lyapunov-based distributed optimization methods for multi-robot coordination, where convergence rates degrade significantly under communication delays and partial observability. We present an enhanced Lyapunov stability framework that incorporates predictive compensation terms to handle asynchronous communication topologies. The key theoretical contribution is a novel composite Lyapunov function that accounts for both optimization dynamics and communication constraints, enabling rigorous stability analysis under realistic network conditions. We derive explicit bounds on the convergence rate as a function of communication delay parameters and demonstrate that the proposed method achieves O(1/k) convergence compared to O(1/√k) for existing approaches. The theoretical results are validated through extensive numerical experiments across random geometric graphs with varying connectivity and delay distributions. Additionally, we extend the framework to handle nonlinear robot dynamics by incorporating feedback linearization techniques, proving input-to-state stability properties. Experimental validation on a team of 12 ground robots performing collaborative transport tasks shows 40% improvement in convergence speed and 60% reduction in trajectory oscillations compared to conventional distributed optimization methods. This work provides theoretically grounded tools for robotic planning in cooperative multi-agent scenarios with practical communication limitations.

We introduce RoboForge, a novel robotic system architecture designed for autonomous assembly in unstructured construction environments. Unlike existing industrial robotic systems that rely on pre-engineered workspaces and explicit CAD models, RoboForge operates on the principle of constructive solid geometry inference, enabling robots to understand and modify incomplete architectural scenes through embodied perception and active reasoning. The system comprises three integrated subsystems: (1) a multimodal perception module combining event-based cameras, thermal imaging, and tactile arrays for robust scene understanding; (2) an uncertainty-aware task planner that reasons about assembly sequences under partial observability; and (3) a compliant manipulation architecture supporting forces up to 150N with 0.1mm positional accuracy. The system design introduces a hierarchical world model representation that continuously updates based on construction progress, allowing real-time replanning when unexpected conditions arise. We deployed RoboForge on three full-scale construction sites over six months, where it successfully completed 847 assembly tasks including structural framing, electrical conduit routing, and finishing work without human intervention. The system demonstrated robust operation across temperature variations from -5°C to 40°C, dusty conditions, and in the presence of human workers. This represents the first demonstration of autonomous robotic construction in real-world environments, establishing a new paradigm for robot applications in the architecture and construction industry.

This paper presents a significantly enhanced human-robot collaboration framework that addresses the critical limitations of existing systems in manufacturing contexts: inability to handle dynamic task reallocation and susceptibility to human motion variability. We design a novel dual-arm robotic workstation with integrated force-torque sensing at 10kHz and an adaptive impedance control architecture that adjusts mechanical impedance based on real-time motion prediction. The system incorporates a hierarchical sensor fusion pipeline combining vision-based skeleton tracking with wearable IMU sensors on human workers, enabling prediction of human intention 350ms ahead of movement execution. The robotic planning module employs a modified优先进程合作(motion) algorithm that guarantees collision-free trajectories while optimizing cycle time under safety constraints. We implemented the system in an automotive assembly line performing door panel installation, conducting a 6-week study with 23 workers across three shifts. Results demonstrate 34% improvement in task completion time, 78% reduction in ergonomically suboptimal movements for human workers, and zero safety incidents across 14,500 collaborative cycles. The system gracefully handles unexpected task modifications such as product variant changes, with reconfiguration time under 45 seconds compared to 15 minutes for conventional programmable logic approaches. This work provides a robust and deployable solution for human-robot interaction in precision assembly, substantially advancing current manufacturing practices.
